Which TWO families fought in the Wars of the Roses?
The House of Lancaster
The House of Stuart
The House of York
The House of Windsor
Lancaster (red rose) and York (white rose).
The House of Lancaster and The House of York
Which battle ended the Wars of the Roses in {#}?
Richard III was killed and Henry Tudor became Henry VII.
What is the symbol of the House of Tudor?
A red rose with a white rose inside it
A white rose
A red rose
A thistle
It shows that the Houses of York and Lancaster were now allies.
Why did Henry VIII establish the Church of England?
The Pope refused to approve his divorce
He wanted to become Pope
Parliament ordered him to
To unite England and Scotland
In the new Church the king, not the Pope, appointed bishops.
Who was Henry VIII’s first wife?
Catherine of Aragon, a Spanish princess; mother of Mary.
Which wife of Henry VIII gave him the son he wanted, Edward?
Jane Seymour died shortly after the birth.
Which TWO wives of Henry VIII were executed?
Anne Boleyn and her cousin Catherine Howard were both executed.
Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard
Which wife of Henry VIII was a German princess he married for political reasons?
He divorced her soon after.
Is the statement below true or false? "Catherine Parr survived Henry VIII."
She was a widow who married Henry late in life, survived him and married again.
Catherine Parr survived Henry VIII.
In whose reign was the Book of Common Prayer written?
Edward VI was strongly Protestant.
Is the statement below true or false? "Elizabeth I avoided serious religious conflict by finding a balance between Catholics and extreme Protestants."
She did not ask about people’s real beliefs.
Elizabeth I avoided serious religious conflict by finding a balance between Catholics and extreme Protestants.
In 1560 the Scottish Parliament abolished the authority of whom?
The Pope
The English king
The clans
Roman Catholic services became illegal in Scotland.
Is the statement below true or false? "The Protestant Church of Scotland established in 1560 was a state Church."
Unlike in England, it was not a state Church.
The Protestant Church of Scotland established in 1560 was a state Church.
For how long did Elizabeth I keep Mary, Queen of Scots, a prisoner?
Mary was eventually executed, accused of plotting against Elizabeth.
What was the name of Sir Francis Drake’s ship?
The Golden Hind
HMS Victory
The Mary Rose
The Mayflower
One of the first ships to sail right around the world.
Stratford-upon-Avon, England.
Which line comes from Shakespeare’s Hamlet?
To be or not to be
Once more unto the breach
All the world’s a stage
A rose by any other name
Once more unto the breach (Henry V); All the world’s a stage (As You Like It); A rose by any other name (Romeo and Juliet).
Who became James I of England, Wales and Ireland in {#}?
James VI of Scotland
Elizabeth I’s cousin. Scotland remained a separate country.
What were the "plantations" in Ireland?
Settlements of Protestant farmers from Scotland and England in Ulster
Tobacco farms
Catholic monasteries
Royal parks
Land was taken from Catholic landholders, with serious long-term consequences.
What was the "Divine Right of Kings"?
The idea that the king was directly appointed by God to rule
The king’s right to choose the Pope
The right of Parliament to remove the king
A tax paid to the Church
James I and Charles I believed in it.
Who were the Puritans?
Protestants who wanted strict and simple religious worship
Supporters of the Catholic Church
The king’s army
Many in Parliament were Puritans who disliked Charles I’s Church reforms.
When did the English civil war begin?
Charles I recalled Parliament in {#}; war began in {#}.
What were the supporters of Parliament in the civil war called?
Jacobites
Whigs
Supporters of the king were Cavaliers.
At which TWO battles was Charles I’s army defeated?
By {#} it was clear Parliament had won.
Marston Moor and Naseby
Is the statement below true or false? "No monarch has set foot in the House of Commons since Charles I tried to arrest five MPs."
The MPs had been warned and were not there.
No monarch has set foot in the House of Commons since Charles I tried to arrest five MPs.
What was England called when it became a republic after 1649?
The Protectorate Kingdom
England declared itself a republic, called the Commonwealth.
What title was Oliver Cromwell given?
King
Lord Chancellor
He ruled until his death in {#}.
Where did Charles II hide after the Battle of Worcester?
In an oak tree
In a church
In Scotland
In the Tower of London
He eventually fled to Europe.
In which year was the monarchy restored with Charles II?
In May 1660 Parliament invited Charles II back from the Netherlands.
Which TWO events happened in London in the reign of Charles II?
A major outbreak of plague ({#})
The Great Fire ({#})
Samuel Pepys wrote about both in his diary.
A major outbreak of plague ({#}) and The Great Fire ({#})
Who designed the new St Paul’s Cathedral?
Edwin Lutyens
After the Great Fire of {#}.
Formed in Charles II’s reign. Members included Halley and Newton.
Which scientist discovered that white light is made up of the colours of the rainbow?
Edmund Halley
Newton also showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.
William of Orange met no resistance and James II fled to France.
Where did William of Orange defeat James II in {#}?
The Battle of the Boyne, in Ireland
Still celebrated by some in Northern Ireland.
What were the supporters of James II called?
Puritans
Some joined him in exile in France.
What did the Bill of Rights of {#} confirm?
The rights of Parliament and the limits of the king’s power
The abolition of slavery
The union with Scotland
It also required the monarch to be Protestant.
Under the Bill of Rights, how often did a new Parliament have to be elected?
At least every three years
Every year
Every five years
Every seven years
Later this became seven years and now it is five.
The beginning of party politics. Conservatives are still called Tories.
They came between 1680 and 1720, persecuted for their religion.
When did the first Jews since the Middle Ages settle in London?
In which year was the Act (Treaty) of Union agreed, creating the Kingdom of Great Britain?
Scotland kept its own legal and education systems and Presbyterian Church.
Which TWO things did Scotland keep after the Act of Union?
Its own legal system
Its own parliament
Its own Presbyterian Church
Its own king
And its own education system.
Its own legal system and Its own Presbyterian Church
Who was the first Prime Minister?
William Pitt
The Duke of Wellington
Prime Minister from {#} to {#}.
This increased his need to rely on ministers, leading to the role of Prime Minister.
Where was Bonnie Prince Charlie defeated in {#}?
George II’s army defeated him; he escaped to Europe.
Who wrote Auld Lang Syne?
Burns, "The Bard", is sung at New Year (Hogmanay).
Adam Smith and David Hume
What was an important principle of the Enlightenment?
Everyone should have the right to their own political and religious beliefs
The king rules by divine right
Only landowners should vote
The Church should control science
The state should not try to dictate beliefs. Still important today.
Which process for mass-producing steel led to the development of shipbuilding and the railways?
The Bessemer process
The Arkwright process
The Watt process
The Spinning Jenny
The Bessemer process.
Richard Arkwright is remembered for what?
The efficient and profitable way he ran his factories
Inventing the steam train
Building canals
Abolishing slavery
He improved the carding machine and used horse-driven and then steam-powered mills.
Who opened the first curry house in Britain?
Robert Clive
Captain Cook
The Hindoostane Coffee House, George Street, London, in 1810.
Who set up the first formal anti-slavery groups?
The Quakers
The Puritans
The Methodists
The Huguenots
In the late {#}s.
In which year did it become illegal to trade slaves in British ships or from British ports?
The 1833 Emancipation Act then abolished slavery throughout the Empire.
What did the Emancipation Act of {#} do?
Abolished slavery throughout the British Empire
Gave women the vote
Made Ireland part of the UK
Abolished rotten boroughs
Afterwards, 2 million Indian and Chinese workers replaced freed slaves.
Which MP played an important part in abolishing the slave trade?
Robert Walpole
Charles Parnell
An evangelical Christian who turned public opinion against the slave trade.
Britain recognised their independence in {#}.
Who commanded the British fleet at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
Nelson was killed. His ship, HMS Victory, is in Portsmouth.
Who defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in {#}?
Known as the Iron Duke, he later became Prime Minister.
When did Ireland become unified with England, Scotland and Wales?
After the Act of Union of 1800, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
Which TWO crosses are on the Union Flag?
The cross of St George
The cross of St David
The cross of St Andrew
The Welsh dragon
And the cross of St Patrick. Wales is not represented.
The cross of St George and The cross of St Andrew
What is the cross of St Andrew?
A diagonal white cross on a blue ground
A red cross on a white ground
A diagonal red cross on a white ground
A yellow cross on a black ground
St George: red cross on white. St Patrick: diagonal red cross on white.
Why is the Welsh dragon not on the Union Flag?
Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was created in 1606
Wales did not want to be included
The dragon was added and later removed
Wales is not part of the UK
The first Union Flag combined the flags of Scotland and England.
How old was Victoria when she became queen in {#}?
She reigned until {#}, almost {#} years.
What was the estimated population of the British Empire at its largest?
More than {#} million
More than {#} billion
The largest empire the world has ever seen.
Between 1870 and 1914, around 120,000 people came to Britain to escape persecution. Who were they?
Russian and Polish Jews
French Huguenots
German Protestants
Many settled in London’s East End and in Manchester and Leeds.
They had prevented the import of cheap grain.
Working conditions gradually improved.
Which engineer built the Great Western Railway?
George Stephenson
It runs from Paddington Station to the south west, the West Midlands and Wales.
Is the statement below true or false? "In the 19th century the UK produced more than half of the world’s iron, coal and cotton cloth."
British industry led the world.
In the 19th century the UK produced more than half of the world’s iron, coal and cotton cloth.
Where did the Great Exhibition of {#} take place?
The Crystal Palace in Hyde Park
Manchester Town Hall
